docs.title: mgsl
docs.text:
mgsl is an implementation of the Metric Gaussian Stochastic Localisation (MGSL) algorithm, written in jax. Broadly, MGSL can be understood as a variational inference (VI) method that produces independent posterior samples. The approximation to the posterior includes all correlations, and does not assume any particular variational family. As such, MGSL is particularly well suited to massive-scale inference problems where the posterior is non-Gaussian, but still unimodal.

The algorithm operates by running localisation "paths". Each of these paths is independent, and produces a single posterior sample.

In a bit more detail, each path follows the observation process \(\mathbf{Y}_\tau = \tau \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{W}_\tau\) where \(\mathbf{X} \sim p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{d})\) is a currently unknown posterior sample, \(\mathbf{W}_\tau\) is a standard Brownian motion process. The observation time \(\tau\) grows until \(\mathbf{Y}_\tau / \tau\) converges to \(\mathbf{X}\). Given \(\mathbf{Y}_\tau = \mathbf{y}\), the unknown follows the localising distribution \(\pi_\tau(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}) \propto p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{d})\, \mathcal N(\mathbf{y} \mid \tau \mathbf{x}, \tau \mathbf{I})\). At every step mgsl approximates \(\pi_\tau\) as a Gaussian, with parameters determined by a matrix-free MGVI fit, and then increments \(\mathbf{y}\) as if \(\mathbf{X}\) were drawn from that Gaussian.

The model must be setup in a particular way to use mgsl. Namely, the parameters must be a single vector with independent standard normal priors on all entries. Typically this is done by using transformations to obtain the priors of interest. The likelihood must also provide its Fisher metric in terms of matrix-vector products. mgsl can work with any jax model, and also works out-of-the-box with nifty.re models through a provided adaptor.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install "git+https://github.com/TomHilder/mgsl.git"
# or
uv add "mgsl @ git+https://github.com/TomHilder/mgsl.git"

(or of course by ssh instead).

jax is a runtime dependency. nifty.re is required if you wish to use the adaptor.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
A simple linear model with Gaussian noise:

from dataclasses import replace

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

import mgsl

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)  # recommended: tighter solver tolerances

n_latent, n_data, sigma = 3, 20, 0.1
A = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (n_data, n_latent))
data = A @ jnp.ones(n_latent) + sigma * jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(1), (n_data,))


def forward(x):  # latent x ~ N(0, I) -> prediction of the data
    return A @ x


lik = mgsl.gaussian(forward, data, noise_std=sigma)

options = mgsl.MGVIOptions(
    n_samples_mgvi=1,  # residual draws per local mgvi fit (doubled in practice via mirror samples)
    n_iter_mgvi=1,  # mgvi rounds per localisation step: (draw residuals, Newton) per step
    newton=mgsl.NewtonOptions(maxiter=5),
)

# Initialise from a longer MGVI fit
fit = mgsl.mgvi_fit(jax.random.key(3), lik, jnp.zeros(n_latent), replace(options, n_iter_mgvi=10))

schedule = mgsl.Schedule(n_paths=256, tau_start=1.0, tau_final=1e5, n_tau=32)
result = mgsl.sample(jax.random.key(4), lik, fit.mean, schedule, options)

result.samples  # (256, 3) NumPy array: posterior samples
result.diagnostics.ess_fraction  # (256, 31): local ESS fraction per path and step
result.failures.totals()  # solver failure counts (always recorded)

There are no defaults for the schedule or for the number of samples and rounds of the local fits: they depend on the problem. This is an active research project and we currently do not have a confident enough understanding of the algorithm to make many recommendations here. The user guide goes into some detail in terms of diagnostics however, and also covers nifty.re models, resuming runs, batches and devices, and power-user options.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to mgsl are documented in this file.

The format follows Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Licence: GNU General Public License v3.0 or later (was MIT).
  • Releases no longer run the tests (they run on pull requests and on main); the docs are deployed with each release.
  • NIFTy.re, a development-only dependency, now comes from PyPI.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• README: installation over HTTPS, documentation link, related work, licence, and how to report problems.
  • Package metadata: project URLs, classifiers, keywords; py.typed marker.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The default line search is now "armijo" (NewtonOptions(line_search=...)); NIFTy.re's line search ("nifty", the previous default) gave up more often on strongly curved posteriors.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Example notebooks in examples/ (a curved 2D posterior; a field seen through binary data, compared with MGVI) and an examples dependency group.
  • Docs workflow: builds the docs on pull requests; deploys to GitHub Pages on manual runs.
  • README: citation section.
First release. MGSL is an in-progress research project: expect bugs, quirks and breaking changes, and see the user guide for what is not yet known about the method.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• sample, and the three steps it chains: init, advance, finalize. Paths start at tau_start from a given centre, advance by drawing the unknown from each step's local Gaussian fit, and end with a terminal local fit.
  • mgvi_fit: MGVI fit of the posterior, e.g. for the starting centre.
  • Likelihood (a pytree: arrays are run-time inputs), gaussian (with mask=) and check_likelihood.
  • Settings: Schedule (all fields required), MGVIOptions (n_samples_mgvi, n_iter_mgvi required), NewtonOptions, CGOptions, grid. Names, defaults and stopping rules follow NIFTy.re's optimize_kl; line_search="nifty" (default) or "armijo".
  • Exact resuming: SLState, save_state, load_state; random numbers derive from the run's key, the path and the global step, so chunked runs equal unchunked ones.
  • Always-on Failures counts with warnings; optional MGSLDiagnostics (local ESS fraction, CG and Newton statistics, terminal fit).
  • Each localisation step is one compiled call, run from a Python loop that prints progress per step; paths run one after another within a call (or batched with vectorize=True), in batches of batch_size, optionally sharded over given devices.
  • Power-user options: a CG preconditioner, Likelihood(fisher_operator=...).
  • mgsl.nifty: from_likelihood, to_samples (NIFTy.re is optional).
  • Conjugate gradients judge convergence on the true residual, recomputed every refresh iterations (CGOptions(refresh=20)) and at apparent convergence, and stop when their objective stops decreasing.
  • Newton-CG with NIFTy.re's line search (default) or a backtracking Armijo search (NewtonOptions(line_search="armijo")).
  • Version from git tags; tagging vX.Y.Z makes a GitHub Release (no PyPI upload yet).

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
The version comes from git tags (hatch-vcs): untagged commits get development versions such as 0.0.2.dev3+g1234abc.

  1. Move the [Unreleased] entries in docs/changelog.md under a new ## [X.Y.Z] - date heading and merge to main.
  2. Tag the merge commit and push the tag:
git tag vX.Y.Z
git push origin vX.Y.Z

The release workflow then builds the sdist and wheel, checks that the version matches the tag, and creates a GitHub Release with the changelog section as its notes and the built files attached; the docs workflow deploys the documentation. The tests run on every pull request and on main (the tests workflow), not in the release. Nothing is uploaded to PyPI yet.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
Under heavy development

MGSL is an in-progress research project, and this code will certainly evolve. Expect bugs, quirks, breaking changes and mistakes. Many properties of the method are still unknown: there is (currently) no principled way to choose the tuning parameters (the number of observation-time steps, and the number of MGVI samples and iterations per step). Essentially nothing is known yet about the error properties of the posterior approximation.

Please report bugs and problems through GitHub Issues, and get in touch before publishing comparisons with MGSL.

docs.title: Why MGSL
docs.text:
• No global variational family. MGSL assumes no global family: it builds a global approximation out of many local Gaussian fits, one per step along each localisation path. It is designed for posteriors that are non-Gaussian.
  • Scales linearly in dimension. Every fit is implicit and matrix-free: we never builds a dense covariance matrix, and use only Jacobian-vector products and conjugate-gradient solves via the Fisher metric. Like typical MGVI, we keep all correlations between parameters (full rank) at a cost only linear in the number of model parameters.
  • Embarrassingly parallel. Each sample comes from its own path, independent of all others. If you have N GPUs (or CPU cores), you can run N samples simultaneously. If your model is cheap this can be worth it on CPU, but generally for larger models it's better to do one sample at a time on CPU.

The most noteworthy (known) limitations are that MGSL is still approximate, and that it does cannot handle multimodal distributions.

Notation: \(\mathbf{x}\) is the latent (dimension \(n\)), \(\mathbf{I}\) the identity, \(\mathbf{J}\) the Jacobian of the forward model, \(\mathbf{F}\) the Fisher metric of the noise model in data space, and \(\tau\) the observation time of the localisation process \(\mathbf{Y}_\tau = \tau \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{W}_\tau\). The localising distribution \(\pi_\tau(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})\) is the posterior distribution of \(\mathbf{x}\) given the observation \(\mathbf{y}\) at time \(\tau\) (NOT the posterior of the original inference problem).

docs.title: Whitened parameter space
docs.text:
mgsl assumes the prior on the latent is \(\mathcal N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\). A model with other priors is written in terms of standard-normal variables through a transformation \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\). The forward model starts from \(\mathbf{x}\):

def forward(x):
    theta = m + L @ x  # provides prior N(m, L L^T) on theta
    return model(theta)  # prediction of the data

docs.title: The likelihood
docs.text:
A Likelihood has

  • log_likelihood(x): \(\log p(\mathbf{d} \mid \mathbf{x})\), up to a constant;
  • fisher(x, v): \(\mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F} \mathbf{J}\,\mathbf{v}\), the Fisher metric projected to the latent space and applied to a parameter vector \(\mathbf{v}\) (e.g. \(\mathbf{F} = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma^2)\) for Gaussian noise); no prior term;
  • fisher_sqrt(x, z): \(\mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F}^{1/2} \mathbf{z}\), which has covariance \(\mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F} \mathbf{J}\) for \(\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\);
  • data_shape: a pytree of jax.ShapeDtypeStruct with the structure, shapes and dtypes of \(\mathbf{z}\) (usually those of the data).

For Gaussian noise, mgsl.gaussian(forward, data, noise_std=..., mask=...) builds all four. noise_std is a scalar or an array of the data's shape. Masked data points (mask False) get zero weight and may hold NaN. For other noise models, the user must provide these properties in a custom likelihood. Alternatively, since nifty.re models are supported, that my be a simpler route.

If you do write a custom likelihood, you can check it is self consistent with mgsl.check_likelihood(lik, x, key). It will error for: a negative log-likelihood is passed as log_likelihood, a data-space Fisher matrix is given instead of \(\mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F} \mathbf{J}\), a \(\mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F} \mathbf{J}\) that is not positive semi-definite, or wrong output shapes. It also warns when the Hessian and \(\mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F} \mathbf{J}\) differ by more than a factor 1.5, a sign of a missing weight or factor (the Hessian is not explicitly formed so this shouldn't be expensive).

Arrays (and Python floats) held by a Likelihood through jax.tree_util.Partial, as gaussian does, are passed to compiled code at run time, so new data of the same shape does not recompile. Arrays captured by a plain closure (a lambda or nested function) are compiled in as constants. Functions, including bound methods, are compared by identity, so a Likelihood rebuilt after its data changed is recompiled rather than run with stale data.

docs.title: NIFTy.re models
docs.text:
import operator

import nifty.re as jft
from jax.tree_util import Partial

import mgsl.nifty

noise_std_inv = Partial(operator.mul, 1 / sigma)  # NIFTy.re takes an operator here
lh = jft.Gaussian(data, noise_std_inv=noise_std_inv).amend(model)  # model: a jft.Model
lik = mgsl.nifty.from_likelihood(lh)
result = mgsl.sample(key, lik, mu, schedule, options)
samples = mgsl.nifty.to_samples(result)  # nifty.re Samples, pos = the sample mean

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
mgsl.sample chains three functions, which can also be called directly:

state = mgsl.init(key, lik, mu, n_paths=256, tau_start=1.0, options=options)
state, report = mgsl.advance(lik, state, mgsl.grid(1.0, 2e4, 64), options)
samples, final = mgsl.finalize(lik, state, options)

The local fits are MGVI Gaussians \(\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})\) of the localising distribution, with centre \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) and precision metric \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = (1 + \tau)\,\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F} \mathbf{J}\) (evaluated at \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\)). A residual is a draw \(\boldsymbol{\delta} \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})\), made by solving \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\delta} = \sqrt{1 + \tau}\,\mathbf{z}_1 + \mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F}^{1/2} \mathbf{z}_2\) with conjugate gradients (CG), for standard-normal \(\mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{z}_2\).

  • init starts each path from \(\mathbf{y} = \tau_0(\boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\delta}) + \sqrt{\tau_0}\,\mathbf{z}\), with \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) a residual at the centre \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) (at \(\tau = 0\)) and \(\mathbf{z}\) standard normal. Small \(\tau_0\) approaches plain stochastic localisation from \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}\); larger \(\tau_0\) skips early steps but relies more on the centre. Check that the centre is converged, e.g. by running mgvi_fit with more rounds and comparing.
  • advance moves every path along a grid of observation times. At each grid point it fits the localising distribution (warm-started from the previous fit) and sets \(\mathbf{y} \leftarrow \mathbf{y} + \Delta\tau\,(\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \boldsymbol{\delta}) + \sqrt{\Delta\tau}\,\mathbf{z}\), with \(\Delta\tau\) the distance to the next grid point. Each step is one compiled call, so grids of any length and values reuse the same compiled code, and progress is printed after every step (progress=False turns it off; the lines also go to the "mgsl" logger):

mgsl  step 12/63  tau=10^2.08  3.41 s  ESS fraction median 0.97, min 0.81  failures 0
- finalize fits each path at its current \(\tau\) and returns \(\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \boldsymbol{\delta}\). It does not change the state. Paths whose log-likelihood became NaN or infinite (counted in failures.nonfinite) get NaN samples.

The run uses the dtype of the centre mu. Float64 (jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)) is recommended; float32 works with looser attainable CG tolerances.

docs.title: Resuming and checkpointing
docs.text:
The state holds everything needed to continue/resume paths. This includes he paths' observations and centres, the observation time and step count, and the run's key and the latent's structure.

mgsl.save_state("run.npz", result.state)
state = mgsl.load_state("run.npz", like=x0)  # x0: a latent (or ShapeDtypeStructs)
state, report = mgsl.advance(lik, state, mgsl.grid(state.tau, 1e5, 16), options)
samples, final = mgsl.finalize(lik, state, options)

load_state raises ValueError if like does not match the saved structure, shapes or dtypes. For crash safety, advance in chunks and save the state after each one (save_state writes atomically, so a crash during a save leaves the previous file intact):

taus = mgsl.grid(state.tau, 2e4, 64)
for k in range(0, 63, 8):
    state, report = mgsl.advance(lik, state, taus[k : k + 9], options)
    mgsl.save_state("run.npz", state)

MGSLDiagnostics.concatenate(a, b) joins the chunks' diagnostics.

This is pretty clunky right now and one of the main areas of improvement for the code base is probably a better and automatic checkpointing system.

docs.title: Paths, batches and devices
docs.text:
• vectorize: within a compiled call, paths run one after another by default, each with as many solver iterations as it needs. vectorize=True batches them with jax.vmap instead, which is faster for cheap models and on accelerators, but every solver loop then runs as long as its slowest path.
  • batch_size: paths per compiled call. By default all paths go in one call and stay on the device between steps; smaller batches bound device memory (they run one after another, and the last is padded, so there is one compilation).
  • devices: shard each batch over exactly these devices. The batch size (default n_paths, padded) must be a multiple of len(devices). Nothing is sharded unless asked.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• Schedule: n_paths, tau_start, tau_final, n_tau (a geometric grid of n_tau points from tau_start to tau_final).
  • MGVIOptions: n_samples_mgvi (residuals per fit, each also used mirrored, \(\bar{\mathbf{x}} \pm \boldsymbol{\delta}\)) and n_iter_mgvi (rounds per fit), both required; Newton and CG settings. Names, defaults and stopping rules follow NIFTy.re's optimize_kl, except the line search: CGOptions(tol=1e-5, atol=0, miniter, maxiter, refresh=20) for the residual draws and NewtonOptions(maxiter, xtol=1e-5, absdelta, cg, adaptive_cg=True, line_search="armijo") for the fits.
  • line_search="armijo" (default): backtracking until a sufficient decrease (Armijo condition) holds, with a steepest-descent fallback for bad Newton directions; it never gives up after a fixed number of tries.
  • line_search="nifty": NIFTy.re's line search (accepts any step that does not increase the objective; restarts along the gradient after six halvings; gives up after nine). On strongly curved posteriors it gives up more often.

docs.title: Choosing the settings
docs.text:
mgsl has no recommended values; check a choice with the diagnostics:

  • The local ESS fraction is expected to sit near its floor at small \(\tau\), where the localising distribution is far from Gaussian. What to look for is the observation time at which the paths' ESS fractions all rise to 1 together: tau_final should be beyond it, so that the terminal fit (result.diagnostics.terminal.ess_fraction) has an ESS fraction close to 1 for every path. If it does not, raise tau_final, e.g. by continuing the state with advance.
  • Failure warnings (capped CG solves, line-search failures) mean the solves are not converged: raise the corresponding maxiter, or check the likelihood.
  • n_iter_mgvi=1 is often enough inside a run, because each fit starts from the previous path's centre; the cold-start mgvi_fit needs more rounds.

docs.title: Power-user options
docs.text:
• MGVIOptions(preconditioner=...): preconditioner(x, tau) returns \(\mathbf{v} \mapsto \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathbf{v}\), with \(\mathbf{M}\) approximating \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = (1 + \tau)\,\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{J}^\dagger \mathbf{F} \mathbf{J}\). x and v are 1-D arrays of length \(n\): the latent flattened as by jax.flatten_util.ravel_pytree. It is built before every group of solves (each round of residual draws and each Newton step), so building it should be cheap. The CG statistics report the residual of the unpreconditioned system.
  • Likelihood(fisher_operator=...), or gaussian(..., linearize_once=True): linearise the forward model once per solve instead of at every Fisher application; costs the memory of the linearisation per path. The returned functions must be pytrees (e.g. jax.tree_util.Partial, or built from the function jax.vjp returns), so that operators at several points can be vmapped.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
result.failures counts, per path, residual and Newton CG solves that stopped at maxiter, CG breakdowns, line-search fallbacks and failures, and fits that started at a non-finite objective ("frozen" paths). It is always recorded, and a warning is issued whenever a count is non-zero. See Failures for what each count means.

result.diagnostics (with calculate_diagnostics=True, the default) holds, per path and step:

  • taus: the observation time of each step's fit;
  • ess_fraction: the effective sample size (ESS) of the fit's \(m = 2\,\)n_samples_mgvi mirrored residuals as importance samples of the localising distribution, rescaled to \((\mathrm{ESS} - 1)/(m - 1)\): 1 means equal weights (the local Gaussian matches the localising distribution at these points), 0 means a single point carries all the weight. Plotted against taus per path, it sits near its floor early on; the convergence check is the observation time at which the paths all rise to 1 together, which tau_final should be beyond. NaN where a residual's CG solve did not converge. It only sees the directions the \(m\) residuals probe: with few residuals it can read close to 1 while the local Gaussian is still off, so judge convergence with a few more residuals than the run itself needs, or on a subset of paths;
  • newton_iter: Newton steps per fit;
  • cg_newton, cg_draws: CGStats of the Newton and residual-draw solves (mean and maximum iterations, largest relative residual, fraction stopped at maxiter);
  • terminal: the same for the final fit that produced the samples.

To create the typical plot to gauge convergence (not correctness), do something like the following:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

d = result.diagnostics
plt.semilogx(d.taus, d.ess_fraction.T, color="k", alpha=0.2)

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Planned work. Nothing is definitely confirmed just a vague plan.

docs.title: Number of MGVI samples varying with τ
docs.text: Different MGVIOptions per advance. Can do awkwardly right now. Maybe not even needed but I suspect it could help on very large problems.

docs.title: Halting on the local ESS
docs.text: Stop once the local ESS fraction has levelled off at 1. Currently only available as a post-hoc check.

docs.title: Complex data
docs.text: Complex-valued data (e.g. radio interferometry) in gaussian and the NIFTy.re adaptor. A good first contribution if you are interested in being involved.

docs.title: Checkpointing during a run
docs.text: Save the sampler state and finished samples as a run progresses (every few τ steps, or as batches finish), so a crashed run restarts from its last checkpoint instead of losing everything.

docs.title: mgsl.Failures
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

Solver failure counts per path, always recorded.

Each field is an integer array of shape (n_paths,), summed over all fits of the call. Non-zero counts mean some results rest on unconverged or failed numerics.

Attributes:

Name Type Description draw_cg_capped array

Residual-draw CG solves that stopped at maxiter: those residuals are too narrow in the directions CG had not reached, and the local ESS of that fit is not computed.

newton_cg_capped array

Newton CG solves that stopped at maxiter (inexact Newton steps; usually harmless if the Newton iteration still converges).

cg_breakdowns array

CG solves stopped by non-positive curvature or non-finite values: the Fisher information is not positive semi-definite or the model returned NaN/inf.

sd_fallbacks array

Newton steps where the CG direction was not a descent direction and steepest descent was used instead.

line_search_failures array

Newton steps where the line search found no decrease although one was predicted.

nonfinite array

Fits whose objective was not finite at the starting centre: the path cannot move ("frozen"), typically NaN data or a log-likelihood undefined there.

docs.title: from_stats(stats) staticmethod
docs.text: From stats with leading axis paths (and any further axes, summed over).

docs.title: totals()
docs.text: Counts summed over paths.

docs.title: warn(where)
docs.text: Issue a warning listing the non-zero counts, with what to check for each.

docs.title: mgsl.MGSLDiagnostics dataclass
docs.text:
Per-path diagnostics of a run (numpy arrays only).

Attributes:

Name Type Description taus ndarray

(n_steps,): the observation time of each step's fit.

tau_end float

Observation time reached after the last step.

ess_fraction ndarray

(n_paths, n_steps), see :class:FitDiagnostics. Over tau, per path, it sits near its floor early on and rises to 1 once the local Gaussian approximation becomes accurate; the convergence check is the tau at which the paths all reach 1 together, which the final tau should be beyond.

newton_iter ndarray

(n_paths, n_steps).

cg_newton, cg_draws CGStats

Fields of shape (n_paths, n_steps).

terminal FitDiagnostics or None

The terminal fit at tau_end that produced the samples (fields of shape (n_paths,)), if the run was finalised.

docs.title: concatenate(a, b) staticmethod
docs.text: Join a run and its continuation along the step axis (terminal taken from b).

docs.title: mgsl.FitDiagnostics
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

Diagnostics of a set of local fits (arrays with leading axis paths).

Attributes:

Name Type Description ess_fraction array

Effective sample size ESS of the fit's m = 2 n_samples_mgvi mirrored residuals as importance samples of the localising distribution, rescaled to (ESS - 1) / (m - 1): 1 means equal weights (the local Gaussian matches the localising distribution at these points), 0 means one point carries all the weight. With few residuals it is a coarse check: deviations of the local Gaussian that the m points do not probe go unseen. NaN where a residual's CG solve did not converge.

newton_iter array

Newton steps taken per fit (all rounds).

cg_newton, cg_draws CGStats

Newton and residual-draw CG statistics.

docs.title: mgsl.CGStats
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

Statistics of the CG solves of each fit (arrays shaped like the fits).

Attributes:

Name Type Description mean_iter, max_iter array

Mean and maximum iterations per solve.

max_rel_residual array

Largest |b - A x| / |b| of the unpreconditioned system.

cap_fraction array

Fraction of solves that stopped at maxiter.

docs.title: mgsl.Likelihood
docs.text:
A likelihood on a latent with a standard-normal prior.

The latent x can be any pytree of real floating-point arrays. The prior on x is always N(0, I): a model with another prior is written in standardised (whitened) coordinates. For example, a parameter z ~ N(m, L L^T) becomes z = m + L x, and a positive parameter with a log-normal prior becomes exp(mu + s x); the forward model then starts from x.

The object is a pytree: arrays it holds (for example data captured by a jax.tree_util.Partial) are passed to compiled code at run time, and everything else (functions, shapes) is static. Functions that close over arrays directly get those arrays compiled in as constants instead.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default log_likelihood callable

x -> log p(d | x), a scalar. Constants may be dropped.

required fisher callable

(x, v) -> J^T F J v: the Fisher metric F of the noise model (e.g. diag(1 / sigma^2) for Gaussian noise) pulled back to the latent by the Jacobian J of the forward model, applied to a tangent v with the structure of x. Must not include the prior.

required fisher_sqrt callable

(x, z) -> J^T F^{1/2} z for z with the structure of data_shape, such that fisher_sqrt(x, z) with z ~ N(0, I) has covariance J^T F J.

required data_shape pytree of jax.ShapeDtypeStruct

Structure, shapes and dtypes of the z taken by fisher_sqrt (usually those of the data).

required fisher_operator callable

x -> (fmv, fsqrt) with fmv(v) = J^T F J v and fsqrt(z) = J^T F^{1/2} z. If given, it is called once per solve and the returned functions are applied inside the solve, instead of fisher(x, .) and fisher_sqrt(x, .). Useful when linearising the model once is cheaper than re-evaluating it at every application; costs the memory of the stored linearisation. fmv and fsqrt must be pytrees (e.g. jax.tree_util.Partial, or built from the function returned by jax.vjp) so that operators at several points can be built and applied with jax.vmap.

None Notes

Functions (including bound methods) are compared by identity when JAX decides whether to reuse compiled code, so a Likelihood rebuilt after its data changed is recompiled. Data held inside a jax.tree_util.Partial are passed at run time and never recompile; data an unchanged function object reads from mutable state are not seen by already compiled code.

docs.title: mgsl.gaussian(forward, data, *, noise_std, mask=None, linearize_once=False)
docs.text:
Gaussian likelihood d = forward(x) + n, n ~ N(0, diag(noise_std^2)).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default forward callable

The forward model, latent x (standard-normal prior) to an array of exactly the data's shape. Must be differentiable and vmappable. Its output is cast to the data's dtype. Compute it in the latent's precision: a float32 forward model with a float64 latent limits the fits to float32 accuracy, which shows up as line-search failures.

required data array

The data. Masked entries may hold any value, including NaN.

required noise_std float or array

Noise standard deviation: a scalar or an array of exactly data.shape. Positive and finite. (NIFTy.re's Gaussian takes the inverse standard deviation instead.)

required mask array of bool

True where a data point is used, shape data.shape. Masked points get zero weight.

None linearize_once bool

If True, also provide fisher_operator, so each solve linearises the forward model once instead of at every application of J^T F J.

False

Returns:

Type Description Likelihood

With the data and weights as run-time arrays.

docs.title: mgsl.check_likelihood(lik, x, key, n_dirs=8, rtol=None)
docs.text:
Check that a likelihood's functions are consistent with each other at x.

Along n_dirs random directions v it compares

  • a = v . fisher(x, v),
  • b = |fisher_sqrt(x, .)^T v|^2 (via jax.linear_transpose), which must equal a,
  • c = -v . H v with H the Hessian of log_likelihood, which for a well-specified model near the data is close to a and always has the same sign.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default lik Likelihood required x pytree

A latent value. Run it at a few points, e.g. zeros (the prior mean) and a fit's centre: the Hessian comparison is most informative near the posterior.

required key Array

Random key for the directions.

required n_dirs int

Number of random directions.

8 rtol float

Tolerance for a == b. Default 1e-6 in float64, 1e-3 in float32.

None

Returns:

Type Description dict

"fisher", "fisher_sqrt" and "hessian": the quadratic forms a, b and c per direction; "hessian_ratio": sum(c) / sum(a).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a function returns the wrong structure or shape, J^T F J is negative along some direction, fisher, fisher_sqrt and fisher_operator (if given) disagree, or the Hessian of the log-likelihood has the opposite sign (e.g. a negative log-likelihood was passed).

Warns:

Type Description UserWarning

If the Hessian-to-Fisher ratio is outside [2/3, 3/2], which suggests a missing weight or factor (or a point far from the data).

docs.title: mgsl.nifty
docs.text:
Adaptor for NIFTy.re (optional: imports nifty.re only when used).

Usage::

import operator

import nifty.re as jft
from jax.tree_util import Partial

import mgsl.nifty

noise_std_inv = Partial(operator.mul, 1 / sd)     # NIFTy.re wants an operator here
lh = jft.Gaussian(data, noise_std_inv=noise_std_inv).amend(model)  # model: a jft.Model
lik = mgsl.nifty.from_likelihood(lh)
result = mgsl.sample(key, lik, mu, schedule, options)
samples = mgsl.nifty.to_samples(result)   # a nifty.re Samples

docs.title: from_likelihood(lh, **primals_kw)
docs.text:
An :class:mgsl.Likelihood from a NIFTy.re likelihood on the standardised latent.

lh must be a likelihood whose primals are the latent with a standard-normal prior, usually likelihood.amend(model) for a NIFTy.re Model. NIFTy.re's energy is the negative log-likelihood, its metric the Fisher metric pulled back to the latent (J^T F J) and its left_sqrt_metric the Fisher square root; they map onto log_likelihood, fisher and fisher_sqrt.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default lh Likelihood

Not a StandardHamiltonian (which already includes the prior).

required **primals_kw

Extra keyword arguments passed to every call of lh's methods.

{} Notes

optimize_kl's point_estimates and constants have no equivalent: fix such parameters inside the forward model instead.

docs.title: to_samples(result)
docs.text:
The samples of an :class:mgsl.Result as nifty.re.Samples.

pos is the sample mean and the samples are stored relative to it, so Samples.at, .pos and NIFTy.re's tools work as for optimize_kl output.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_paths int

Number of independent paths, i.e. of posterior samples.

required tau_start float

Localisation time at which the paths start (> 0).

required tau_final float

Localisation time the paths reach; the terminal fit that produces the samples is made there.

required

docs.title: taus property
docs.text: The grid, float64 array of shape (n_tau,).

docs.title: mgsl.MGVIOptions dataclass
docs.text:
Settings of the local MGVI fits made at every step.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_samples_mgvi int

Number of residual draws per fit. Each is mirrored, so the fit averages over 2 * n_samples_mgvi points (NIFTy.re's n_samples with mirror_samples=True). Required.

required n_iter_mgvi int

Number of rounds (draw residuals, then Newton) per fit. Required.

required newton NewtonOptions

Newton-CG settings. Required (its maxiter has no default).

required draw_cg CGOptions

Stopping rules of the CG solves that draw residuals.

CGOptions() preconditioner callable

preconditioner(x, tau) returning a function v -> M^{-1} v, where M approximates the matrix the CG solves invert, the precision metric Lambda = (1 + tau) I + J^T F J at the current centre x (J the Jacobian of the forward model, F the Fisher metric of the noise model). x and v are 1-D arrays of length d: the latent flattened as by jax.flatten_util.ravel_pytree. It is called before every group of solves: once per round of residual draws and once per Newton step, so building it should be cheap compared with a solve. It may be a pytree (e.g. jax.tree_util.Partial) whose array leaves are passed at run time rather than compiled in.

None

docs.title: mgsl.NewtonOptions dataclass
docs.text:
Stopping rules of the Newton-CG minimisation in each local fit.

The minimisation stops after maxiter steps, once the step taken has 1-norm <= xtol * d (d the latent dimension), or once the objective decreased by less than absdelta. Names, defaults and these stopping rules are those of NIFTy.re's Newton-CG. Differences: the inner CG starts from whichever of zero and the step that ignores the likelihood (y / (1 + tau) - x) has the smaller residual (NIFTy.re starts from zero), and stops on its residual only (NIFTy.re also stops it on the decrease of the CG objective), so it may take more iterations per solve.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default maxiter int

Maximum number of Newton steps per round. Required.

required xtol float

Step-size tolerance, multiplied by the dimension d.

1e-5 absdelta float

Stop when the objective decreased by less than this. Off by default.

None cg CGOptions

Iteration limits of the inner CG solves (and their tolerances if adaptive_cg is False).

CGOptions() adaptive_cg bool

If True, the inner CG stops at a residual 1-norm of min(0.5, sqrt(|g|_1)) |g|_1 for gradient g (an inexact Newton method), ignoring cg.tol and cg.atol.

True line_search ('armijo', 'nifty')

"armijo" (default): halves the step until the objective decreases by at least 1e-4 times the decrease predicted by the gradient (the Armijo condition), down to a step of 1e-12; a Newton direction that is not a descent direction (or not finite) is first replaced by steepest descent capped at length sqrt(d); a step is kept only if the objective strictly decreased. It never gives up after a fixed number of tries. "nifty" (NIFTy.re's line search): tries steps 1, 1/2, 1/4, ... along the Newton direction and takes the first that does not increase the objective; after six failures it restarts along the gradient (scaled by g.g / g.H.g); after nine it gives up and the centre stays put. absdelta only applies when fewer than two halvings were needed. On strongly curved posteriors it gives up more often than "armijo".

"armijo"

docs.title: mgsl.CGOptions dataclass
docs.text:
Stopping rules of a conjugate-gradient solve.

The solve stops once the residual 2-norm is below max(tol * |b|, atol), after at least miniter and at most maxiter iterations. Names and defaults are those of NIFTy.re's conjugate gradients. CG tracks its residual by a recurrence that drifts from the true residual b - A x in floating point; the true residual is recomputed every refresh iterations and whenever the solve looks converged (one extra application of A each), so convergence is always judged on the true residual.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default tol float

Tolerance relative to the norm of the right-hand side b.

1e-5 atol float

Absolute tolerance on the residual norm.

0 miniter int

Minimum number of iterations. Default min(6, maxiter).

None maxiter int

Maximum number of iterations. Default min(200, 20 d) for a latent of dimension d.

None refresh int

Iterations between recomputations of the true residual (NIFTy.re uses 20). Without them, badly conditioned solves drift and can end far from the solution; but each refresh also perturbs the CG recurrence, so refreshing very often (every few iterations) slows convergence. Each refresh costs one extra application of A.

20

docs.title: mgsl.sample(key, lik, mu, schedule, options, *, calculate_diagnostics=True, batch_size=None, devices=None, vectorize=False, progress=True)
docs.text:
Draw schedule.n_paths posterior samples with MGSL.

Chains :func:init (at schedule.tau_start from centre mu), :func:advance (over schedule.taus) and :func:finalize. The samples are approximate: each step replaces the localising distribution by a local Gaussian fit. For a linear model with Gaussian noise and converged solves they are exact.

The run uses the dtype of mu (float64 needs jax_enable_x64; float32 works, with looser attainable solver tolerances).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key Array

Random key (typed or legacy).

required lik Likelihood required mu pytree

Centre the paths start from, e.g. mgvi_fit(...).mean. Its structure, shapes and dtypes define the latent.

required schedule Schedule required options MGVIOptions required calculate_diagnostics bool

Record the local ESS and the CG and Newton statistics. Costs 2 n_samples_mgvi + 1 log-likelihood evaluations per fit. Failure counts are recorded either way.

True batch_size int

Paths per compiled call; batches run one after another and the last one is padded. Default: all paths in one call, kept on the device between steps. Smaller batches bound device memory.

None devices sequence of jax devices

Shard each batch over exactly these devices (batch_size must be a multiple of their number; by default all paths, padded to a multiple). Default: no sharding, whatever devices exist.

None vectorize bool

False (default): within a call, paths run one after another, each with as many solver iterations as it needs. True: paths are batched with jax.vmap, which is faster for cheap models or on accelerators, but every solver loop then runs as long as its slowest path.

False progress bool

Print one line per step to stderr (time, local ESS fraction, failure count). The same lines go to the "mgsl" logger at INFO level.

True

Returns:

Type Description Result

docs.title: mgsl.init(key, lik, mu, *, n_paths, tau_start, options, batch_size=None, devices=None, vectorize=False)
docs.text:
Start n_paths localisation paths at tau_start.

Each path starts from y = tau_start (mu + delta) + sqrt(tau_start) z, with z standard normal and delta ~ N(0, Lambda^{-1}) a draw from the Gaussian approximation at mu, whose precision metric is Lambda = I + J^T F J at mu (see :func:advance). Each path's first local fit is warm-started at mu. If N(mu, Lambda^{-1}) were the exact posterior, y would follow the exact localisation process at tau_start. Solver failures of these draws are reported by a warning.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key Array

Random key of the run (typed or legacy). All later random numbers derive from it.

required lik Likelihood required mu pytree

Centre the paths start from, e.g. mgvi_fit(...).mean.

required n_paths int required tau_start float

Localisation time to start at (> 0).

required options MGVIOptions

Only draw_cg (and the preconditioner) are used here.

required batch_size int | None

See :func:sample.

None devices int | None

See :func:sample.

None vectorize int | None

See :func:sample.

None

Returns:

Type Description SLState

docs.title: mgsl.advance(lik, state, taus, options, *, calculate_diagnostics=True, batch_size=None, devices=None, vectorize=False, progress=True, _warn=True)
docs.text:
Advance every path of state along the grid taus.

At each grid point tau the path's localising distribution is fitted by MGVI, warm-started from the previous centre. The fit is a Gaussian N(xbar, Lambda^{-1}) with precision Lambda = (1 + tau) I + J^T F J at xbar (J the Jacobian of the forward model, F the Fisher metric of the noise model). The observation then moves to the next grid point, dtau later, as if the unknown were a draw from that Gaussian: y += dtau (xbar + delta) + sqrt(dtau) z, with delta ~ N(0, Lambda^{-1}) and z ~ N(0, I) fresh for every step and path.

Each step is one compiled call (for all paths, or per batch), so the grid's length and values do not cause recompilation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default lik Likelihood required state SLState required taus array

Increasing grid; taus[0] must equal state.tau (relative tolerance 1e-12). Use mgsl.grid(state.tau, tau_final, n) for a geometric continuation.

required options MGVIOptions required calculate_diagnostics bool

See :func:sample.

See :func:sample.

True progress bool

See :func:sample.

Fits each path's localising distribution at state.tau and returns xbar + delta, with xbar the fit's centre and delta ~ N(0, Lambda^{-1}) a draw from it (see :func:advance). The state is not changed, so it can still be advanced further and finalised again. Samples of paths whose fit hit a non-finite log-likelihood are NaN.

docs.title: mgsl.mgvi_fit(key, lik, x0, options)
docs.text:
MGVI fit of the posterior (no localisation), e.g. to find the centre paths start from.

Runs options.n_iter_mgvi rounds; each draws options.n_samples_mgvi mirrored residuals at the current centre and runs Newton-CG on the sample-averaged negative log posterior. A fit of the full posterior from a cold start usually needs more rounds than the warm-started fits inside a run, e.g. dataclasses.replace(options, n_iter_mgvi=10). Check convergence, e.g. by comparing the centre after more rounds.

docs.title: mgsl.SLState dataclass
docs.text:
State of a set of localisation paths at one observation time.

It holds everything needed to continue the paths: :func:mgsl.advance continues them and :func:mgsl.finalize draws samples from them. Random numbers are derived from the run's key, the path index and the global step, so a run split into several :func:mgsl.advance calls gives the samples of one uninterrupted run over the same grid points with the same options (bit for bit with the same batch_size, devices and vectorize; to rounding otherwise).

(n_paths, d): the accumulated localisation observation of each path (flat latent).

Localisation time.

step int

Number of steps taken since the start.

Raw data of the run's random key.

Name of the key's PRNG implementation.

Structure of the latent.
